title: Radio data for 1958-1993 reject a separate 10.5% F10.7 step at January 1981 under stable spectral relations
abstract: We test whether a separate F10.7 calibration step can explain the January 1981 change in the sunspot-to-radio relation. We use 13,037 common observation days in 1958-1993 from Canadian F10.7 and Japanese radio flux at 2 and 3.75 GHz. In 1978-1983, their direct spectral ratio changes by +0.33% (95% six-month block interval -1.13% to +1.83%). A model with activity level and spectral slope gives +0.79% (-0.09% to +1.74%). The flux above 67 SFU changes by +1.45% (-0.17% to +3.04%). A model fitted to 1958-1978 predicts withheld F10.7 in 1981-1982 with RMS log error 0.0177. A 10.5% downward correction of total flux or active flux increases this error to 0.1083 or 0.0725. At matched radio activity, a cycle-phase test gives a sunspot-number fall of 12.8% in Cycle 21 and 14.1% in Cycle 20, before the Zurich-to-Brussels transfer. Cycle 22 gives a smaller, uncertain fall. These results oppose a large F10.7-only step but do not prove a sunspot calibration error. The broad multi-frequency interpretation was published in 2024; this work adds quantitative bounds, withheld-year correction tests, and an earlier phase control. Limits include solar spectral variation, shared Japanese calibration, a 1979 receiver change, few independent blocks, and only three phase controls. External data and record-level derivatives remain outside this baseline package.

display.caption: Six estimates of the separate F10.7 change at January 1981, using 1978-1983 data and 95% six-month block intervals. The dashed line is a 10.5% total-flux gain hypothesis. Spectral stability is an assumption.
Error in 1981-1982 from a radio model fitted on 1958-1978. Both defined 10.5% correction rules increase prediction error.
Sunspot-number changes at matched radio activity in 24-month windows before and after dates 13 months past each cycle maximum. A comparable drop occurs before the 1981 production change.
